title: Pentecostals and charismatics
hookLine: Azusa Street, 1906: the fastest-growing Christians today, praying with gifts of the Spirit

lines: SIDE BY SIDE, PRAYING FOR HOURS.
cards: Los Angeles, April 1906. A run-down building on Azusa Street, once a church, lately a stable and a storeroom. Sawdust on the floor.
Planks across nail kegs for benches. The preacher is William Seymour, a Black man, the son of formerly enslaved parents, blind in one eye.
Night after night, people crowd in: Black and white, Mexican, Asian, rich and poor, side by side, in an America where that almost never happened. They pray for hours.
Some weep, some shout, some fall silent, and some begin praying in languages they don't know. Newspapers mock them. Visitors come from across the world and go home changed.

teach.b: Pentecostals take their name from Pentecost, the day in Acts 2 when the Holy Spirit came on the first disciples: "And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance."
Pentecostals believe the same Spirit still gives the same gifts today: speaking in tongues, healing, prophecy, a word of wisdom.
Paul lists these gifts in First Corinthians 12 and calls them charismata, gifts of grace. That's where charismatic comes from.
Pentecostals belong to churches born from this movement, like the Assemblies of God or the Church of God in Christ.
Charismatics are Christians in other churches, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Baptist, who from the 1960s on began praying this way too, while staying in their own churches.
Together they may be something like a quarter of all Christians on earth, most of them in Africa, Latin America and Asia.
Their worship is often loud, joyful and long, with hands raised, and a strong sense that God is close and acting now.
Others see it differently: some believe certain gifts, like tongues, ended with the apostles; many welcome the gifts but pray more quietly. The churches hold that disagreement openly.
And a sad footnote to Azusa: within a few years, many Pentecostal churches divided along racial lines, like the rest of America.

teach.h: AS THE SPIRIT GAVE THEM UTTERANCE.
teach.b: But one short prayer is shared by nearly every church: a medieval Latin hymn, Veni Sancte Spiritus, begins, come, Holy Spirit.

how: Pentecostal and charismatic worship is often long and lively, with raised hands, spontaneous prayer, praying in tongues, and prayer for healing, while many charismatics also worship within Catholic, Anglican and other churches.

o: a church office held only by bishops
a magnetic personality that draws people in
gifts of grace the Spirit gives, like healing

games.q: what's inside the words — tap the pairs.

s: charismatics must leave their church to join a Pentecostal one
charismatics pray this way while staying Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Baptist and more.
most Pentecostals and charismatics today live in the United States
most live in Africa, Latin America and Asia.
the word charismatic comes from Paul's word for gifts of grace

games.q: it's 1906, Los Angeles. at the Azusa Street meetings, people of every race are sitting side by side. what happens to the movement over the next few years?
o: many of its churches divide along racial lines.
games.why: within a few years many Pentecostal churches divided by race, like the rest of America. yet the movement itself grew around the world.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and notice the difference from clenched hands: open hands can't grab or hold on; they can only receive.

If you pray, say three words slowly on the breath, come, Holy Spirit, then wait, without asking for anything in particular. If you don't pray, just sit with your hands open, ready for whatever the day gives.

wordCard.voice: Charismata. Paul's word for gifts of grace in Greek, the root of charismatic: a gift the Spirit still gives today.

orig.note: Greek: a gift of grace, from charis, grace. Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 12, the root of charismatic.

carryVoice: Your line: come, holy spirit. Gifts of grace, still given. Day two hundred ninety-five, done.
